ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The acetic acid structure on the left side of the figure contains a carboxylic acid group, and C=O as well as the adjacent O–H can be seen; when two molecules are arranged opposite each other, the O–H of one molecule faces the carbonyl oxygen of another molecule. The acetyl chloride structure on the right side of the figure contains C=O and Cl, but has no O–H bond. Reasoning: Forming a stable dimer requires relatively strong intermolecular attraction. An acetic acid molecule has both an O–H hydrogen-bond donor and a carbonyl oxygen as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, so two acetic acid molecules can mutually form two strong hydrogen bonds, obtaining a stable cyclic dimer. Acetyl chloride has no O–H hydrogen and cannot donate a hydrogen bond like acetic acid, so two acetyl chloride molecules mainly can only rely on weaker dipole-dipole interactions to attract each other. Therefore acetic acid forms a dimer more easily than acetyl chloride.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: the acetic acid structures show an O–H group next to a C=O group, while the acetyl chloride structures show C=O and Cl but no O–H bond. Then reason from intermolecular forces: each acetic acid molecule can donate its O–H hydrogen to the other molecule’s carbonyl oxygen and accept a hydrogen bond at its own carbonyl oxygen, giving a stable cyclic dimer with two strong hydrogen bonds. Acetyl chloride lacks the O–H hydrogen needed to donate such bonds, so two acetyl chloride molecules can only align polar bonds for weaker dipole-dipole interactions. Therefore acetic acid forms dimers better.
